paragraphs.heading: A limit on fraction roots
paragraphs.text: The rational root theorem puts a limit on which fractions can solve a polynomial equation whose coefficients are all integers, with the first and last coefficients not zero. The solutions of such an equation are also called the roots or zeros of the polynomial. The rule goes by several names, among them the rational zero test and the p/q theorem.

paragraphs.heading: Why it helps
paragraphs.text: Its job is to find every rational root a polynomial has, if it has any. Instead of an endless supply of fractions, it hands you a finite list of candidates, and each one can be checked. When a candidate r works, you can divide the factor (x – r) out using polynomial long division. What is left is a polynomial of lower degree, and its roots are also roots of the original.

paragraphs.heading: Where the candidates come from
paragraphs.text: Suppose p/q is a root written in lowest terms. Multiplying the equation through by qⁿ clears the fractions. Moving the constant term across and pulling out p shows that p times a whole number equals −a₀ qⁿ. Since p and q are coprime, Euclid's lemma says p must divide the constant coefficient a₀. A matching rearrangement, pulling out q instead, puts q next to the leading coefficient aₙ.

paragraphs.heading: Two quick examples
paragraphs.text: Take 2 x³ + x − 1. A reduced root would need a top that divides 1 and a bottom that divides 2, so the only options are ± 1/2 and ± 1. None of them makes the polynomial zero, so it has no rational roots. For x³ − 7 x + 6, the candidates are ±1, ±2, ±3 and ±6. Of these, 1, 2 and –3 work, and since a cubic has only three roots, those are all of them.

paragraphs.heading: Cutting the work down
paragraphs.text: For 3 x³ − 5 x² + 5 x − 2, any rational root must be one of eight numbers: ± 1, ± 2, ± 1/3, ± 2/3. Testing all eight can be tedious, but a few tricks let you skip some of them. When x is negative every term of this polynomial is negative, so the sum cannot be zero and only the four positive options remain. P (1) works out to 1, and a short check rules out 2. In the end only P (2 / 3) has to be computed, and x = 2 / 3 turns out to be the one rational root.

paragraphs.heading: Solving cubics without cube roots
paragraphs.text: Any cubic equation whose coefficients are integers has three solutions, counted in the complex plane. If the test finds no rational solution, the only algebraic way to write the solutions uses cube roots. If it does find one, r, dividing out (x – r) leaves a quadratic. The quadratic formula then gives the other two roots, with no cube roots needed.

paragraphs.heading: Its family
paragraphs.text: The theorem is a special case of Gauss's lemma on factoring polynomials, the case of a single linear factor. When the leading coefficient aₙ equals 1, the result is called the integral root theorem.
